meta.reportLabel: Sun - JACKSON HOLE WEEK. Warsh gives his FIRST speech as Fed Chair on Friday Aug 28 at 14:00Z, and core PCE lands two days earlier on Wednesday forecast to ACCELERATE to 0.3% m/m with GDP revised lower. Correction to Thursday's file: Jackson Hole is Aug 27-29, NOT Aug 27 - the event is still ahead of us. Friday extended everything: GOLD 4,608 (+1.80% on the day, ~+5% on the week, highest since mid-May), SILVER 68.99, WTI 87.06, BRENT 94.39, DXY 98.68 at a THREE-MONTH LOW. EUR/USD 1.1678, GBP/USD 1.3648, USD/JPY 158.94. Two upgrades: JAPAN goes -1 to 0 - July national CPI landed at 1.9% with core 1.8%, the highest since March, exactly the print that decides September 18. And CHF goes 0 to +1 - Q2 GDP +1.5% q/q, a RECORD trade surplus of CHF 8.1bn, services PMI 63.9 and ZEW +10 from -25, on top of the haven bid. COPPER finally joined the metals, +1.63% Friday on China restocking, so XCU comes off RANGE to a LOW-MED LONG. Canada retail sales printed -0.8%. Iran still refuses talks, Oman mediation 'positive but at risk', blockade intact, Hormuz flow 8-9mb/d on dark transits. Cleanest trades: XAU LONG, USOIL LONG, EUR/USD LONG, USD/CHF SHORT, DXY SHORT. Size DOWN into Friday - Warsh is a genuine two-way risk.

meta.regime: The debasement trade that the Treasury's buyback expansion lit on Wednesday ran all the way through Friday's close and is now the dominant regime: long US real rates falling with the policy rate unchanged, which is the cleanest possible combination for gold and against the dollar. Gold settled 4,608 and silver 68.99, the dollar index is 98.68 at a three-month low, and the energy shock underneath has not eased at all - Brent settled 94.39 with the US naval blockade of Iran still in force and no negotiations under way. What changes this week is that the regime finally meets a scheduled test: core PCE on Wednesday and Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote as Fed Chair on Friday, into a market that has no policy record to anchor on.

dailyRead: This is a positioning file, not a data file, and it has one job: get you into Jackson Hole week with the right size and the right corrections already made. Start with the correction, because Thursday's file got the date wrong. It said Jackson Hole was Aug 27 and treated it as the single reversal risk sitting just ahead. The symposium actually runs August 27 to 29 and Kevin Warsh's first keynote as Fed Chair is on FRIDAY August 28, with core PCE on Wednesday August 26 as the warm-up. That matters for sizing: you have three full sessions of regime before the risk event, not one. Now the tape. Friday extended every leg of the debasement trade rather than fading it. Gold settled at 4,608 dollars, up 1.80% on the day and roughly 5% on the week, its highest since mid-May. Silver settled 68.99, up 1.15%. WTI settled 87.06 and Brent 94.39, both higher again. The dollar index closed near 98.68, a three-month low, down more than 0.8% on the week. EUR/USD is 1.1678, GBP/USD 1.3648, USD/JPY 158.94. The mechanism has not changed since Wednesday: the Treasury doubled its liquidity-support buyback operations for longer-dated bonds, the long end of the US curve broke lower from a nineteen-year high, and long real rates are the single most important input into both the gold price and the value of the dollar. Nothing that happened Friday argued against it. Two upgrades follow, and both are data-driven rather than mood. JAPAN goes from -1 to 0. The July national CPI that Thursday's file flagged as 'the decider' landed and it landed hawkish: headline 1.9% from 1.6%, core 1.8% from 1.6% and the highest since March, core-core 1.9% from 1.7%, Tokyo core 1.9% and Tokyo headline 2.0%, services inflation 1.2%, goods 2.7%, food 3.5%. That is the print the market needed to hold roughly 62% pricing for a hike to 1.25% on September 18, and it delivered. The counterweight is real and is why this is a move to zero rather than to positive: the import price index printed a RECORD 200, terms of trade fell again to 81.62, and the July trade balance widened to MINUS 634 billion yen from -410 billion. Brent at 94 makes each of those worse every month. But USD/JPY at 158.94 is comfortably below the 160 line where the MoF has already demonstrated it will intervene, and the rate-differential story is now moving toward the yen rather than against it. SWITZERLAND goes from 0 to +1, and this is the bigger reassessment. Thursday's upgrade to zero was a positioning call about the haven bid. The Swiss data now supports something stronger. Q2 GDP came in at +1.5% quarter-on-quarter, the strongest since 2021, led by chemicals and pharma with services also expanding. The July trade surplus was a RECORD 8,141 million francs against 3,834 million, with exports 27,790 million. The services PMI jumped to 63.9 from 59.8. The ZEW economic sentiment index swung to +10 from MINUS 25. The current account is 7.1% of GDP. That is not a funding-currency data set. The two things holding CHF at +1 rather than higher are the policy rate at exactly zero with CPI at 0.4% and core 0.3%, and the fact that SNB foreign exchange reserves ROSE to 768,260 million francs in July from 758,851 million - which is the Bank leaning against precisely this appreciation. Treat SNB intervention as the named invalidator on every franc long. USD/CHF has broken below 0.80 and stays a HIGH-conviction short. New Zealand goes to +1, completing the rehabilitation that started Tuesday. The OCR was raised to 2.50% on July 8, the Committee said further increases appear likely, Governor Breman then escalated that in a speech to 'sooner and more sharply than previously indicated', and the September 2 Monetary Policy Statement is now widely expected to deliver another 25bp. The survey side has turned hard with it: business confidence 56.1 from 36.6, ANZ Roy Morgan consumer confidence 99.3 from 91.3, GDT +2.3%. Q2 CPI at 4.1% is above the 1-3% band with core 3.2%. The drag is still there - unemployment 5.6%, wage growth only 2.1%, the July trade balance blowing out to -1,949 million from -237 million - which caps the kiwi at +1 rather than +2. Canada stays +1 but only because of oil. The activity side deteriorated again: retail sales printed -0.8% month-on-month against +0.6%, the composite PMI is 49.7 and services 49.1 with both in contraction, annual GDP growth is -0.1% and the terms of trade fell to 101. Against that, the inflation case is genuinely strong - CPI 3.0%, energy inflation 16.6%, producer prices +12.4% y/y, CPI-common 2.7%, services 2.5% - and the labour market is the G10's best with +75,100 jobs and unemployment at a two-year low of 6.4%. WTI at 87.06 with Brent at 94.39 is doing the heavy lifting; keep CAD long against the dollar and the yen, and drop conviction on the non-oil crosses. Australia holds at 0. The July labour survey break has not been repaired: employment fell 15,827, unemployment is 4.5% and the post-COVID high, participation slipped to 66.9%. But consumer inflation expectations ROSE to 4.9% in August from 4.7%, consumer confidence jumped to 88.9 from 83.9, commodity prices are +15.4% y/y and the cash rate at 4.35% is still the highest in the G10. Genuinely mixed. Europe keeps +2 and is still the best-supported score on the board: July HICP 2.9% with core UP to 2.5%, services 3.3%, energy HICP 10.0%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, the August flash composite PMI at 52.1 with manufacturing 52.8 from 51.9, ZEW 31.4, and TE calling the September 10 hike almost fully priced with only a material easing in energy prices able to change it - Brent at 94 is not that. The deposit facility is re-verified at 2.25%, not the 2.40% refi headline. Sterling holds +1 on the 3.75% Bank Rate, the 6-3 vote and the G10-highest gilt, but the hawkish case keeps thinning: services inflation cooled to 3.4% from 3.6% and wage growth to 4.1% from 4.4%. The dollar stays -2 with the caveat that Friday is a coin-flip. Non-farm payrolls printed MINUS 23,000 in July, CPI eased to 3.4% and core to 2.5%, and the FOMC minutes were hawkish and ignored. Warsh has deliberately abandoned heavy forward guidance, told reporters his remarks would focus on long-term structural questions, and described the speech as 'a blank piece of paper' - which means the market has no roadmap and the distribution of outcomes is wide in both directions. With crude at 87 he still has an energy argument available for a hawkish framing. Finally, the commodity complex. Copper was the outlier on Thursday and stopped being one on Friday, rising 1.63% on China restocking and tight spreads to roughly 6.58-6.61 dollars a pound; XCU comes off RANGE to a LOW-MED LONG and that also strengthens the industrial leg under silver. USOIL stays a HIGH-conviction long: no US-Iran negotiations, an Iranian military leader publicly vowing Tehran 'will not submit' and that oil will not pass the strait, the US planning a further economic squeeze, three ADNOC vessels hit by missiles and drones this month, and Hormuz throughput running only 8-9 million barrels a day on dark transits with transponders off. The practical instruction for the week: hold the direction, cut the size into Wednesday, and do not carry full risk through 14:00Z Friday.

USD.when: Sept 16-17 FOMC (hold the base case - but Warsh speaks Friday Aug 28 first)
USD.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE this morning at 3.75% upper bound (3.50-3.75%), held on Jul 29 in a 9-3 vote with three presidents dissenting for a quarter-point hike. TE data unchanged since Thursday: CPI 3.4% from 3.5% and a five-month low, core 2.5% from 2.6%, Q2 GDP 1.5% annualised with annual growth 2.1%, unemployment 4.1% from 4.2%, non-farm payrolls MINUS 23,000 from +20,000, average hourly earnings +0.1% m/m, August flash composite PMI 56.0 from 54.5 with services 56.8 from 54.6. The week's structure is what matters now. Wednesday Aug 26 brings the second estimate of Q2 GDP alongside PCE, with core PCE forecast to ACCELERATE to 0.3% m/m while GDP is revised lower - a hot-inflation, slowing-growth pairing that is genuinely awkward for a Fed with three hawkish dissenters on record. Then Friday Aug 28 at 14:00Z, Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote as Chair. He has deliberately moved away from the heavy forward guidance of the previous regime, told reporters on Jul 29 that the remarks would focus on long-term structural questions rather than near-term guidance, and described the speech as 'a blank piece of paper right now'. Roughly 69% of surveyed fund managers expect a neutral tone. That is precisely why the risk is two-way and wide: there is no policy record to anchor on, and with crude at 87.06 he retains an energy argument for a hawkish framing at any moment he chooses. The dollar short stays on at -2 through Wednesday; carry reduced size through Friday.

EUR.when: Sept 10 (TE: almost fully priced - and Brent at 94 is not 'easing energy')
EUR.note: Deposit facility re-verified on TE at 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike, with main refinancing at 2.40% and marginal lending at 2.65%. Use the 2.25% depo, never the 2.40% headline. The case is unchanged and remains the most self-supporting on the board: July HICP 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5% from 2.4%, services inflation 3.3% from 3.2%, energy HICP accelerating to 10.0% from 8.5%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, the August flash composite PMI at 52.1 with manufacturing 52.8 from 51.9 and services 51.7, wage growth 3.4% from 3.1%, unemployment stable at 6.3%, and the euro-area ZEW at 31.4 in August from 23.4. TE calls the September 10 move almost fully priced and states that only a material easing in energy prices would change that view - Brent settled at 94.39 on Friday, so that condition is nowhere close to met. Lagarde's stated logic is that the longer energy stays elevated the more likely it drives broader inflation through indirect and second-round effects, and the Canadian July CPI is the hard proof of that channel operating. The July meeting accounts have now been published and did not soften the pricing. Standing cautions: consumer inflation expectations eased to 2.9% from 3.0%, producer prices decelerated to 4.6% y/y, retail sales -0.3% m/m and food inflation only 0.8%. France and Spain print CPI on Friday Aug 28 as the pre-read for the Sept 1 euro-area flash. EUR/USD 1.1678.

GBP.when: Sept 17 (Jul 30 = 6-3 hold; the hawkish evidence keeps thinning)
GBP.note: Bank Rate re-verified on TE at 3.75%, held Jul 30 but 6-3 with a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus. Both decisive prints have landed and both cut the same way once you look past the headline. The labour report: wage growth eased to 4.1% including bonuses from 4.4%, employment change fell to +83,000 from +147,000, unemployment held at 4.9% against expectations of a fall to 4.8%, and the claimant count FELL 11,000 after a 6,400 fall. July CPI rose to 2.9% from 2.6%, the first increase in the annual rate since March, but the driver was administered energy on the Ofgem cap adjustment; core CPI held FLAT at 2.6% and services inflation COOLED to 3.4% from 3.6%. The activity picture is decent but decelerating: Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q with the annual rate up to 1.2% but the quarterly rate down from 0.6%, August composite PMI 52.5 from 52.2. The 10-year gilt near 5.1% is still the G10's highest and is doing more for sterling than the MPC is. GBP holds +1, but with services inflation falling and wages easing the three dissenters are running out of evidence, and another Ofgem adjustment arrives in October. Express sterling against the yen, the dollar and the Aussie rather than against the euro or the franc. Cable 1.3648.

JPY.when: Sept 18 (~62% priced - and Friday's CPI delivered exactly what that pricing needed)
JPY.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 1.00%, held Jul 31 in an 8-1 vote with Takata dissenting for 1.25%. UPGRADE from -1 to 0. The July national CPI that Thursday's file called the decider printed hawkish across the board: headline 1.9% from 1.6% and the highest since December 2025, core 1.8% from 1.6% matching consensus and the highest since March, core-core 1.9% from 1.7%, Tokyo core 1.9% and Tokyo headline 2.0%, services inflation 1.2% from 1.1%, goods 2.7% from 2.2%, food 3.5% from 3.2%, PPI 7.2%, inflation expectations 2.7%. Core is still below the 2% target for a sixth month, but the direction is what the September pricing needed and it got it. The July Summary of Opinions was already the most hawkish document of this cycle, with one member saying the pace of hikes could EXCEED market expectations and another that the cost of delay is not insignificant. The domestic case is the best in three decades: June labour cash earnings +3.4% y/y, real earnings +1.6% and positive for a sixth month, unemployment 2.5%, jobs-to-applications 1.18, June industrial output +1.9% m/m and +4.9% y/y, machinery orders +9.7% m/m and +16.9% y/y, the August Reuters Tankan at 18 from 13, manufacturing PMI 55.1 and services 52.3. What holds this at 0 rather than +1 is the external account, which is deteriorating with Brent: the import price index printed a RECORD 200, import prices +29.1% y/y, terms of trade down to 81.62 from 82.71, and the July trade balance out to MINUS JPY 634bn from -410bn, with imports +27.8% y/y against exports +23.2%. USD/JPY 158.94 is comfortably clear of the 160 line where the MoF has already acted, so intervention risk is currently low but not zero. Tokyo August CPI lands Thursday Aug 27 at 23:30Z.

AUD.when: Sept 29 (hold - the hawkish hold lost its labour-market justification and has not got it back)
AUD.note: Cash rate re-verified on TE at 4.35%, held unanimously on Aug 11 with Governor Bullock revealing the Board did NOT discuss a cut at all - only whether to raise or hold. That frame was damaged by the July labour force survey and has not recovered. Employment FELL 15,827 against a consensus of plus 20 to 25 thousand; full-time rose 16,333 but part-time collapsed 32,160. Unemployment rose to 4.5% from 4.4%, the highest of the post-COVID era. Participation fell to 66.9% from 67.0% and the employment-to-population ratio to 63.9%, so the rise in unemployment understates the deterioration. Job vacancies fell to 330,000 from 338,000, the terms of trade dropped to 112 from 117, business confidence is -6 and the current account deficit is a record -AUD 27.1bn. What keeps AUD at 0 rather than negative is the price side and the rate itself: 4.35% is still the G10's highest, Q2 weighted median CPI ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5%, trimmed mean to 3.6% from 3.5%, services inflation 4.0% from 3.7%, headline 3.8%, and consumer inflation expectations ROSE AGAIN to 4.9% in August from 4.7%. Commodity prices are +15.4% y/y, consumer confidence jumped to 88.9 from 83.9, and copper joining Friday's rally helps the terms-of-trade read at the margin. August PMIs are still expansionary at 52.5 composite. Genuinely mixed, and that is the honest verdict. RBA Meeting Minutes land Tuesday Aug 25 at 01:30Z and are the week's only Australian catalyst worth positioning for.

NZD.when: Sept 2, 02:00Z (another 25bp widely expected - Breman: 'sooner AND more sharply')
NZD.note: OCR re-verified on TE at 2.50% after the 25bp hike on Jul 8, the first in three years, taken by consensus. UPGRADE from 0 to +1. The Monetary Policy Committee framed the July move as a step to return inflation to the middle of the 1-3% band and explicitly said further OCR increases appear likely at upcoming meetings, with timing highly uncertain. Governor Anna Breman then escalated that in a speech, saying the OCR is likely to rise SOONER AND MORE SHARPLY than the Bank had previously indicated - a deliberate hardening of the guidance rather than a restatement of it. The September 2 Monetary Policy Statement is now widely expected to deliver another quarter-point, and the survey side has turned hard to meet it: business confidence JUMPED to 56.1 in July from 36.6, ANZ Roy Morgan consumer confidence to 99.3 from 91.3, the Global Dairy Trade index +2.3% in August after +0.1%, and food inflation eased to 1.9% from 2.5%. The price backdrop justifies the Bank: Q2 CPI accelerated to 4.1% from 3.1%, well above the target band, with core at 3.2% and the RBNZ projecting a 4.3% peak in Q3. What caps this at +1 rather than +2 is that the hard data is still the G10's weakest: unemployment 5.6% and the highest since Q3 2015, wage growth only 2.1%, youth unemployment 17.2%, the manufacturing PMI down to 54.3 from 60.1, services PMI 50.6, and the July trade balance blowing out to MINUS NZD 1,949m from -237m as imports jumped to 9,340m. Two-year inflation expectations are only 2.34%. NZD/USD near 0.60. The Sept 2 decision is the kiwi's whole story.

CAD.when: Sept 2, 13:45Z (hold - the PMIs and retail sales both argue against the hike camp)
CAD.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 2.25%, held Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting. CAD stays +1, but understand that oil is carrying it. The inflation case is genuinely strong: July CPI rebounded to 3.0% from 2.8%, at the ceiling of the 1-3% control range, with energy inflation accelerating to 16.6% from 14.3% on gasoline and every core measure higher - CPI-median 2.0% from 1.9%, CPI-trim 1.9%, CPI-common 2.7% from 2.6%, core ex food and energy 2.3% from 2.1%, services 2.5% from 2.2%, goods 3.7% from 3.5%. Producer prices are running +12.4% y/y. The labour market is the G10's best: July employment +75,100, the largest gain in two years, full-time +38,600, unemployment down to a two-year low of 6.4%, participation 65.1%. Against all of that, the activity side keeps deteriorating and got worse on Friday: retail sales printed MINUS 0.8% m/m against +0.6% previously, the composite PMI is 49.7 and services 49.1 with both in CONTRACTION, annual GDP growth is -0.1% with the quarterly rate at 0.0%, the terms of trade fell to 101 from 107 despite the oil move, business confidence slipped to 55.1 from 56.2, and house prices are -2.3% y/y. A central bank already near the lower end of its estimated neutral range will not tighten into contracting services activity whatever the CPI prints, and wage growth at 3.4% gives it no reason to. The asymmetry still runs away from cuts, which is why CAD stays positive, but express it against the DOLLAR and the YEN where the oil leg does the work, not on the non-oil crosses. WTI 87.06, Brent 94.39. Canadian GDP lands Friday Aug 28 at 12:30Z, into the Warsh session.

CHF.when: Sept 24 SNB (zero through 2027 - but the data no longer looks like a funding currency)
CHF.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 0.00%, next assessment September 24, TE's model at 0.00% through 2027 and consensus seeing no hike before 2028. UPGRADE from 0 to +1, and unlike Thursday's move this one is data-led rather than positioning-led. The Swiss real economy just printed a very strong quarter: Q2 GDP +1.5% quarter-on-quarter against +0.4%, the strongest since 2021, driven by industry with the chemical and pharmaceutical sector the largest contributor and services also expanding. The July trade surplus hit a RECORD CHF 8,141 million against 3,834 million, with exports 27,790 million and imports falling to 19,649 million. The services PMI jumped to 63.9 from 59.8. The ZEW economic sentiment index swung to +10 from MINUS 25. Business confidence rose to 104 from 102, industrial production +5.5% y/y after -7.6%, and the current account is 7.1% of GDP. On top of that sits the haven bid: USD/CHF has broken and held below 0.80 in the same week that US 30-year yields collapsed and gold gained ~5%. Two things cap this at +1. First, the monetary side is unchanged and is that of a funding currency - July CPI 0.4% from 0.5%, core 0.3%, producer and import prices deflating at -2.1% y/y, unemployment up to 3.0% from 2.9%, wage growth 1.8%, the SNB's own inflation forecast 0.6% for 2026 and 2027. Second, and more actionable: SNB foreign exchange reserves ROSE to CHF 768,260 million in July from 758,851 million. The Bank is buying foreign currency against exactly this move, and it flagged in June that Middle East tensions could strengthen the franc and signalled greater readiness to intervene. Treat SNB intervention as the named invalidator on every franc long. Some of the GDP strength is also pharma front-running of US tariffs and will not repeat.

catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz / Iran-US escalation watch
catalysts.note: No negotiations under way; Oman's mediation described as positive but at risk from continued vessel attacks. Blockade intact, throughput 8-9mb/d on dark transits. Drives USOIL, CAD, JPY and the haven complex simultaneously.

Reserves ROSE to CHF 768,260m in July from 758,851m. The Bank is buying foreign currency against franc strength and has signalled readiness to do more. This is the named invalidator on every CHF long.
USD/JPY at 158.94 is clear of the 160 line where the Ministry has already acted, so risk is currently low. A hawkish Warsh that pushes the pair back toward 160 puts it live again.

geopolitics: The Iran-US conflict is now a settled, high-level plateau rather than an escalating spiral, and that plateau is exactly what keeps the risk premium in the price. There are no negotiations under way. An Iranian military leader publicly vowed this weekend that Tehran 'will not submit' and that oil will not be allowed to pass through the Strait of Hormuz or the Persian Gulf, while claiming Iran has still shipped 70 million barrels in the past one to two months despite the blockade. Washington is preparing a further economic squeeze rather than a diplomatic opening, and President Trump has said he will 'never apologize' for the military action, arguing that higher gasoline prices have been worth it. Oman continues to mediate and describes the talks on navigation as 'positive and constructive', but has warned explicitly that Iran's continued targeting of vessels puts any progress at risk - three ADNOC tankers have been hit by missiles and drones in the strait this month. The US Department of Energy puts throughput at 8 to 9 million barrels a day, well below pre-war levels, sustained by 'dark transits' in which chartered tankers switch off transponders, run the strait to the Gulf of Oman and offload to waiting vessels; crossings did rise 27% over the past week, which is the only de-escalatory data point on the page. The FX transmission is unchanged and runs four ways at once. It keeps Brent at 94.39 and WTI at 87.06, which is a direct CAD tailwind and the sole reason the loonie holds +1 despite retail sales at -0.8% and both PMIs below 50. It is the mechanism behind euro-area energy HICP at 10.0% and Canadian energy inflation at 16.6%, which is what makes the Sept 10 ECB hike almost fully priced. It is the single largest drag on the yen through a record import price index of 200, terms of trade at 81.62 and a July trade balance of minus JPY 634 billion - the one thing working against Friday's hawkish CPI print. And it underwrites the haven bid in gold at 4,608, silver at 68.99 and a franc that has broken below 0.80 against the dollar. Trade it as a persistent condition, not a headline: the de-escalation scenario that unwinds USOIL, softens the ECB's case and relieves the yen all at once runs through Muscat, and there is no sign of it yet.
